A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same clipping-bound and batch-size study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including matching retained analyses across appendix renumbering. Some new experimental settings are internally inconsistent, but this does not prevent a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original private fine-tuning experiments, accuracy sweeps, gradient distributions, and per-class analyses on SUN397, Cassava, and CIFAR-100, including its 10% subset.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds image and text LoRA experiments, training from scratch, DP-SGD, full-parameter fine-tuning, and additional gradient analyses.

M1.justification: The clipped and noisy updates, joint hyperparameter tuning, and cumulative-noise/minimum-step batch-size rule remain unchanged. LoRA, DP-SGD, and full fine-tuning are additional experimental settings. Section 5.1 explicitly states that the revised optimal-clipping theorem is explanatory and is not used to select clipping bounds during training.

E1.justification: v2 adds 20 Newsgroups text classification and CIFAR-10 classification in Appendices G.2 and I.1. This substantially extends coverage beyond v1's image transfer-learning datasets. SUN397, Cassava, and both CIFAR-100 data regimes remain represented.

E2.justification: AUTO-S with gamma 0.01 remains the evaluated competing clipping method in Figure 5 and the corresponding accuracy table. The prior batch-size heuristics are also retained. Added architectures, optimizers, and parameterizations test the analysis under different settings rather than introduce competing hyperparameter-selection methods.

E3.justification: New protocols include image LoRA, DistilBERT LoRA with sequence length 512, full-parameter fine-tuning, DP-SGD, and WideResNet training from scratch. Table A3 adds a rank sweep with C fixed to 1. Existing FiLM protocols largely remain. The added scratch experiment's actual budget is unclear: Figure A18's title says 40 epochs, whereas its caption and surrounding text say 8.

E4.justification: v2 adds LoRA-rank sensitivity, per-class clipping analyses across additional training regimes, and investigation of full fine-tuning as an exception to the main trend. Figure 3 and Appendices J and L add gradient-distribution and mean-gradient trajectories during training. Earlier Cassava and CIFAR-100 per-class analyses remain in Appendix K.

E5.justification: New Figure A13 reports medians across three repeats with min–max bands, adding a different aggregation practice from v1's mean-based accuracy comparisons. Existing three- and five-seed reporting and min–max bands are retained; the PDFs do not establish increased replication of the existing experiments.

E6.justification: v2 adds accuracy grids for LoRA, text classification, training from scratch, DP-SGD, and full fine-tuning. New Table A3 reports, for example, accuracies of 0.4107 and 0.3800 for LoRA ranks 1 and 16 at epsilon 0.5. Full fine-tuning produces a new exception favoring large clipping bounds in both difficulty regimes. All 15 AUTO-S comparison rows are unchanged between v1 Table A3 and v2 Table A4.

T1.justification: v2 removes v1's inverse-cubic clipping/noise scaling derivation. The revised optimal-clipping theorem adds an explicit bounded-domain assumption and possible optima at individual gradient norms. New Theorem 5.4, Corollary 5.5, and Appendix E connect gradient MSE to a bound on optimization progress under smoothness and step-size assumptions.

C1.justification: The abstract's headline claims and batch-size contribution remain unchanged. Contribution 2 now explicitly claims a connection between optimal clipping and optimization progress. The conclusion replaces an expectation of transfer to full-model tuning with demonstrated LoRA extensions and a full-fine-tuning exception, refining the contribution's scope.

C2.justification: v1 expects the core findings to transfer to full-model tuning; v2 explains that full fine-tuning can favor large clipping bounds in both easy and hard settings, proposing increased parameter count and gradient norms as the mechanism. It also states that operationalizing the optimal-clipping theorem would require additional privacy mechanisms and discusses the small clipping effects observed on the text task.

D1.justification: Table A1 and Appendices G and I substantially expand reproducibility information with optimizer-specific grids, LoRA ranks and placement, trainable-parameter choices, and text sequence length. However, the explicit Opacus implementation attribution and SUN397/Cassava ResNet-50 grid rows disappear. These are documentation changes, not evidence that the underlying implementation or those earlier runs changed.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for LoRA, DistilBERT, WideResNet, scaling rules, and feature-quality research, including discussion of Wang et al. and Zhao et al. It changes the linear-scaling attribution from Tramer and Boneh to Panda et al. and reframes the limitations of Koloskova et al.'s bound. The broader clipping and batch-size positioning remains intact.

P1.justification: The abstract, main section order, and much existing prose remain intact. Local rewrites clarify problem difficulty, revise the theoretical motivation and conclusion, and expand methodological explanations. The appendices separate the prior bound from proofs and organize the added experiments; publication headers and acknowledgments also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds a practical-guidance table, a LoRA-rank table, and extensive new heatmaps, per-class plots, histograms, and training trajectories. Figure 3 changes from final-gradient violins to epoch-wise distributions; Figure 5 redisplays unchanged accuracies as differences from the best. Table A1 gains a method column, and Algorithm 1 is relocated and reformatted.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important theoretical and applicability weaknesses: it removes v1's invalid inverse-cubic derivation, qualifies the optimal-clipping theorem, and proves a connection to optimization progress. Broader experiments test generality and replace speculative full-model extrapolation with an explicit empirical exception. New reporting inconsistencies, notably the 8-versus-40-epoch discrepancy in Figure A18, limit reproducibility of some additions, but the theoretical repairs and better-supported applicability boundaries provide a substantial net improvement.
